content: The recommended dosage of ursodiol for treatment is 8-10 mg/kg/day, administered orally in divided doses every 8-12 hours, with a maximum dose of 300 mg per administration. For maintenance therapy, a dose of 250 mg orally at bedtime for six months is suggested, or 300 mg orally twice daily. In some cases, a dosage of 13-15 mg/kg/day, divided every 6-12 hours with food, may be prescribed. Ursodiol has orphan drug designation for the treatment of cystic fibrosis-related liver disease and Niemann-Pick disease type C. Following the Kasai procedure, a dosage of 10-20 mg/kg/day, divided every 8-12 hours, is recommended. Aluminum hydroxide and calcium carbonate can reduce the effectiveness of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism, so caution and monitoring are advised. Crofelemer may increase ursodiol levels by inhibiting transporters MRP2 and OATP1A2 in the gut, though systemic inhibition is unlikely due to minimal absorption. Ethinyl estradiol, sodium bicarbonate, sodium citrate/citric acid, cholestyramine, colesevelam, colestipol, and mestranol can decrease the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism, requiring caution and monitoring. Gallstone dissolution with ursodiol may take several months, and recurrence of stones can occur within five years in up to 50% of patients. Adverse effects of ursodiol include headache, dizziness, diarrhea, dyspepsia, nausea/vomiting, back pain, upper respiratory tract infections, alopecia, rash, hyperglycemia, flatulence, peptic ulcers, urinary tract infections, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, cholecystitis, fatigue, abdominal pain, pruritus, angioedema, peripheral edema, biliary pain, and hepatobiliary disorders such as jaundice or worsening of pre-existing jaundice. Abnormal laboratory findings may include increased ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and gamma-GT levels. Gastrointestinal disorders such as abdominal discomfort, enteroliths (bezoars), and constipation have also been reported. Gallstone complications requiring surgery, hypersensitivity reactions, and biliary gastrointestinal fistulas are possible. Ursodiol should only be used for radiolucent, non-calcified, high-cholesterol-content gallstones. Caution is advised in patients with chronic liver disease, non-visualizing gallbladders, or those requiring cholecystectomy. Liver function tests should be monitored every three months for the first three months of therapy and every six months thereafter. Therapy should be discontinued if clinically significant increases in liver function parameters occur. In pregnant women, available data from randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and case series over several decades have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Ursodiol is naturally present in human milk, and while no adverse effects on breastfed infants have been reported, data are limited. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential risks to the infant. Ursodiol is a naturally occurring bile acid that reduces cholesterol secretion from the liver and decreases the fractional reabsorption of cholesterol in the intestines. It has a bioavailability of 90%, with an initial response for gallstone dissolution observed within 3-6 months. Approximately 70% of the drug is protein-bound. Ursodiol is rapidly taken up by the liver, conjugated with glycine or taurine, and excreted in bile. Non-absorbed ursodiol is metabolized in the colon to lithocholic acid. Metabolites include glyco-ursodeoxycholic acid, tauro-ursodeoxycholic acid, and inactive compounds such as 7-keto-lithocholic acid and lithocholic acid. A small portion is metabolized to sulfate-conjugated lithocholic acid, which is excreted in bile and eliminated in feces. The primary route of excretion is through feces.
